brief.head: Blame the state
brief.text: Monopolies do not arise in a free mar­ket with proper com­pe­ti­tion, Amit Varma ar­gued. They come from state in­ter­fer­ence shield­ing a crony, or from the state it­self. {060-C06}

brief.head: Resist easy wins
brief.text: Big prob­lems are slow and hard to credit, so many re­searchers re­treat to small ones they can solve. Amit Varma’s ad­vice to the young: keep your eye on the tar­get. {060-C10}

brief.head: The CEO as superstar
brief.text: We credit a su­per­star CEO like Jack Welch for what a dis­persed or­gan­i­sa­tion achieved, Amit Varma said, and we make the same mis­take with heads of gov­ern­ment. {060-C14}

brief.head: A day is your life
brief.text: Grand goals are toxic, Amit Varma said: achieve one and grander ones ap­pear. A day is not a wait­ing room for life to hap­pen. A day is your life. {060-C16}

brief.head: Not a restaurant
brief.text: At a restau­rant ev­ery­one or­ders what they like. In a democ­racy, out­voted din­ers eat seafood or go hun­gry. Hence, Amit Varma said, the need for a re­pub­lic. {060-C19}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why states aren’t firms
lead.head: A firm hand, the wrong job

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 60

body: Amit Varma opened with a “light triad” to set against the dark triad of se­rial killers: three words be­gin­ning with F. They were firms, fi­nance and free­dom. {060-J01}

Firms, both hosts agree, are awe­some. That is the trou­ble. It is a short step to think­ing that some­one who has run a good firm, or ad­vised one, could run a coun­try bet­ter than “ran­dom extra politi­cians”.
“That is a ter­ri­ble, ter­ri­ble fal­lacy,” Varma said, born of a top-down in­stinct from our hunter-gatherer past.
The episode drew on a chap­ter of *In Service of the Republic*, by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah: a coun­try is not a com­pany.
“At the end, gen­tle reader, we hope to per­suade you that the two skills are re­ally com­pletely apart,” Shah said. {060-C01}
He bor­rowed a friend’s anal­ogy: firms are cells, and the econ­omy is the or­gan­ism. There is no pros­per­ity with­out healthy firms, but what works for a cell does not work for the body.
## Counting the ways
First, feed­back. A firm sees its stock price daily, its pro­duc­tion weekly and its prof­its monthly, so mis­takes show up within months.

Government has no such score­card: the stock index says lit­tle about the econ­omy, and GDP comes quar­terly and late. “Firms can work well and have a bet­ter chance at work­ing well be­cause there are feed­back loops and they get slapped into shape,” Shah said. {060-C03}

Second, sur­vival. A firm can go bank­rupt; a min­istry can­not. “If you are the de­fence min­istry of India, you are the de­fence min­istry of India,” Shah said. “You could lose wars, many things could go wrong, but ba­si­cally your life is as­sured.”
Third, co­er­cion. A firm is a raft of vol­un­tary con­tracts. The state holds a mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence; it is, Shah said, “a co­er­cive crea­ture”.
Fourth, com­plex­ity. Shah, who knows both worlds, finds firms clean and solv­able be­side government’s tan­gle of de­part­ments and ob­jec­tives.

Fifth, rules. A small firm can hus­tle from deal to deal, but a state that bar­gains with each cit­i­zen of­fers “rule of men”, not rule of law, and “the path­way to in­fi­nite cor­rup­tion”. {060-C12}
Sixth, power. A small firm can be run by one boss; a state must split power be­tween branches and be­tween lay­ers of gov­ern­ment.

Seventh, time. India, Shah said, is on a hun­dred-year jour­ney to close a 9x gap with America in per capita GDP. Every re­form must pass through a pol­icy pipe­line that is, in his word, in­ex­orable. {060-C15}
## Business is not banned

None of this makes busi­ness peo­ple unfit to gov­ern, Varma in­sisted. Flexible thinkers such as Paul Graham, Naval Ravikant or Jeff Bezos could change how they think. The “stan­dard issue McKinsey con­sul­tant”, he added, was an­other mat­ter.
Nor are politi­cians nat­u­ral gov­er­nors. Many mas­ter the game of re­tail pol­i­tics, Varma said, then find that gov­er­nance and pol­icy are dif­fer­ent games al­to­gether.

Shah, a great ad­mirer of what India’s firms have achieved since the early nineties, called their best peo­ple world class. But their skills, he warned, do not trans­fer straight into pub­lic pol­icy. Varma named the bias: the halo ef­fect.

Shah’s book of the day, *When McKinsey Comes to Town* by Walt Bogdanich and Michael Forsythe, came with a cau­tion: “the book is a bit mean, it’s a bit one-sided.” Still, he said, it shows how hard it is to bring a con­sult­ing ap­proach to the com­plex prob­lems of pub­lic pol­icy.

second.label: Social science
second.head: A penny in a stormy pool
second.deck: Amit Varma on why governments cannot run clean experiments

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the coin in the stormy pool

body: Social sci­ence is not like the phys­i­cal sci­ences, Amit Varma said, and he had an anal­ogy from his friend Shruti Rajagopalan, who may have had it from Don Boudreaux. In a lab­o­ra­tory, test­ing whether a coin dis­places water is easy: mea­sure a beaker, drop the coin in gen­tly, mea­sure again.
Now try it in a crowded swim­ming pool, a hun­dred me­tres by a hun­dred, with a storm over­head and forty peo­ple swim­ming and throw­ing things. Everything is mul­ti­causal. {060-C04}

A busi­ness choos­ing be­tween two blends of polyester can run an A/B test and tin­ker its way to an an­swer, Varma said. {#polyester} A gov­ern­ment is in the pool, and is not even sure what it is mea­sur­ing.

quote.text: There is a storm over­head, there are forty peo­ple swim­ming in­side and throw­ing things, and you’re try­ing to drop a coin there.

third.head: Catastrophe, then a rally

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the COVID stock rally

body: COVID was a ter­ri­ble catas­tro­phe, Ajay Shah said. Yet when the US Fed and the RBI cut rates sharply, stock prices went up. {060-S01}
Firms were not sud­denly being run bet­ter. “It was re­ally about a new in­ter­est rate for com­put­ing NPVs,” he said: the same fu­ture prof­its, dis­counted at a lower rate.

So no­body, he said, should mis­take the stock mar­ket index for a re­port card on the econ­omy or the gov­ern­ment. Stock prices are not “non in­for­ma­tive non­sense”: there is a lot of sense in what they do. They sim­ply do not re­port the health of the econ­omy.
That leaves a coun­try with­out the daily score­card a firm en­joys. In pub­lic pol­icy, Shah said, “It’s a lit­tle bit of fly­ing blind.” {#blind}

box.title: The chapter behind the show
box.text: The episode fol­lows a chap­ter of *In Service of the Republic*, by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah. All the points are made there, Amit Varma said, “beau­ti­fully writ­ten”. The video is a com­pan­ion: “but please read.” {#chapter}

sections.label: First difference
sections.head: The feedback that never comes
sections.caption: feedback loops
body: A firm lives in­side a loop of in­for­ma­tion, Ajay Shah said. It watches its mar­ket share, its rev­enue, its prof­its and its stock price, which comes out daily. When some­thing goes wrong, man­age­ment hears about it within months.
So a firm need not be run by a big thinker. It can debug its way for­ward, solv­ing one small prob­lem after an­other. That does not pro­duce great leaps, Shah said, but it keeps the firm going.

Government has no such loop. GDP, at its best, is a quar­terly num­ber with a con­sid­er­able lag, and in India its mea­sure­ment has run into many dif­fi­cul­ties. Mistakes can “per­pet­u­ate dam­age week after week and month after month”. In gov­ern­ment, Shah said, there are no such feed­back loops. {060-C03}
## Votes are not ver­dicts
Elections, he added, come once every five years and are only mildly re­lated to per­for­mance, and base pas­sions still weigh dis­pro­por­tion­ately in win­ning them. {#elections}
Amit Varma saw the op­po­site prob­lem: with state and local polls al­ways round the cor­ner, elec­tions are in ef­fect hap­pen­ing all the time, and they drive short-termism.

Even the sig­nal vot­ers send can point the wrong way. Agriculture needs deep struc­tural change, which takes years and can­not quickly be cred­ited to any­one. A farm loan waiver wins votes now, and has be­come a hy­giene fac­tor that ev­ery­body of­fers.
~ Sometimes, Varma con­ceded, dis­tress is so great that a waiver is needed. But it is an anaes­thetic, not a cure.

quote.text: A waiver like that can be a nec­es­sary anaes­thetic, but it is not the struc­tural change you need.

sections.label: Second and third
sections.head: The ministry that cannot die
sections.caption: monopoly and coercion
body: In a pri­vate firm, Ajay Shah said, bank­ruptcy is al­ways on the table. A min­istry has no such worry: even a de­fence min­istry that loses wars is as­sured of its life. {060-C05}
For many state bod­ies, he said, mo­nop­oly means not su­per­nor­mal prof­its but un­ques­tioned co­er­cive power, and with­out the fear of death comes com­pla­cence.

Amit Varma went fur­ther. In a free mar­ket with proper com­pe­ti­tion, he said, a mo­nop­oly is im­pos­si­ble. Monopolies come from state in­ter­fer­ence that shields a crony, or from the state it­self, with its mo­nop­o­lies on vi­o­lence and money. {060-C06}
Market fail­ure, he added, is in­cred­i­bly rare. Government fail­ure is ubiq­ui­tous.
## A raft of con­tracts

A firm, Shah said, is a set of vol­un­tary con­tracts with cus­tomers, em­ploy­ees and other firms. The few that hire gun­das are scummy, and their peo­ple be­long in jail. The state, in Max Weber’s def­i­ni­tion, holds a mo­nop­oly of phys­i­cal vi­o­lence in a ter­ri­tory. {060-C07}
Varma added the dou­ble thank you, John Stossel’s phrase for a vol­un­tary ex­change that leaves both peo­ple bet­ter off. The state has no need to earn a thank you: it takes what it wants. {060-C08}
~ The same per­son, Varma said, faces very dif­fer­ent in­cen­tives at the head of a firm and at the head of a gov­ern­ment. As Lord Acton said, power cor­rupts. {060-J13}

quote.text: That to be the state is to have co­er­cive power.

sections.label: Fourth difference
sections.head: Shoot first, think later?
sections.caption: complexity and the bias for action
body: Even a large firm is sim­ple next to gov­ern­ment, Ajay Shah said, which spreads across many de­part­ments and of­fices, with dif­fer­ent ob­jec­tives, each pulling its own way.
Having worked in both worlds, he finds firms clean and solv­able, and gov­ern­ment so com­pli­cated that you must scale back even the am­bi­tion of mea­sur­ing and un­der­stand­ing it. {060-C09}
## A bias for ac­tion?

That led to the episode’s open dis­agree­ment. Shah has grown un­com­fort­able with a favourite slo­gan of star­tups and ven­ture cap­i­tal, a bias for ac­tion, even in busi­ness. Shooting first and ask­ing ques­tions later is su­per­fi­cial, he said, and in gov­ern­ment “truly dan­ger­ous”. {060-C11}
Policy needs thought first: what is the mar­ket fail­ure, what is the low­est-cost in­ter­ven­tion, and how will it re­shape in­cen­tives and sur­vive the po­lit­i­cal econ­omy?

Amit Varma agreed about the state. About firms, he said, “I can’t dis­agree more strongly with that.” Great com­pa­nies start out doing one thing, then it­er­ate and pivot, a les­son he drew partly from the es­says of Paul Graham. {060-R06}
They agreed it is not a bi­nary. Jeff Bezos, Varma said, had a bias for ac­tion and was also a deep thinker. Shah’s real tar­get, he sug­gested, was re­flex­ive short-termism.
~ Varma in­vited view­ers to ask for a full episode on the ques­tion, though Shah, he joked, might de­cline: “That will be bias for ac­tion.” {060-J05}

quote.text: Whereas with gov­ern­ment, it is like, my God, this is too hard. This is im­pos­si­bly com­pli­cated.

sections.label: Fifth difference
sections.head: No haggling with the state
sections.caption: rules versus deals
body: A firm may live from deal to deal, Ajay Shah said. It can agree to de­liver nickel of a cer­tain grade for six months at a cer­tain price, de­liv­ery point Shanghai. {#nickel}

Government can­not work that way. Its many arms need pol­icy co­her­ence across time and across or­gan­i­sa­tions, or one will con­tra­dict an­other. And a state that strikes deals with pri­vate per­sons of­fers rule of men, not rule of law. {060-C12}
Its job, Shah said, is to set sta­ble rules that re­shape in­cen­tives, so that pri­vate peo­ple can make long-term plans. It should not be mak­ing steel or a pay­ment sys­tem.
## The fran­chise les­son

Large firms dis­cover rules too. McDonald’s could strike a dif­fer­ent deal with every fran­chisee, since no Article 14 binds it to equal treat­ment. In prac­tice it of­fers a stan­dard con­tract, or it would fall apart in com­plex­ity and cor­rup­tion. {#mcdonalds}
The state, the most com­plex or­gan­i­sa­tion of all, is bound by Article 14. It can­not give one cit­i­zen one deal and an­other a dif­fer­ent one.
Shah had lit­tle pa­tience for talk of a China model, in which a Fortune 500 chief flies in to shake hands with a strong­man. That, he said, should em­bar­rass us. {060-J03}
~ Amit Varma added that firms adopt rules as they scale, from Six Sigma to Google’s motto of “do no evil”.

quote.text: The en­gage­ment be­tween a gov­ern­ment and a pri­vate per­son can ab­so­lutely not be deals.

sections.label: Sixth difference
sections.head: Octopus beats starfish
sections.caption: the dispersion of power
body: In a five-man firm, Ajay Shah said, the CEO can be “a lit­tle demigod” while the oth­ers cower. But past any mean­ing­ful scale, a firm run by one per­son telling ev­ery­body what to do is guar­an­teed to be medi­ocre.

A friend gave him an image for this. A tiny firm is like cook­ing: the cook chooses gar­lic or onions. A grow­ing one is gar­den­ing, where you cre­ate con­di­tions, cul­ture and in­cen­tives, and run a port­fo­lio of bets. {#gardening}
In a coun­try as di­verse as India, he added, even a firm should not be a starfish with one brain at the cen­tre, but an oc­to­pus, with think­ing peo­ple all over. {#starfish}
## No choice for the state
For the state, Shah said, there is no op­tion: the only way known to make a gov­ern­ment work is to dis­perse power. {060-C13}

So the state is split into leg­isla­tive, ex­ec­u­tive and ju­di­cial branches, and into a union gov­ern­ment, “a lit­tle con­fused crea­ture called a state gov­ern­ment”, and city or vil­lage gov­ern­ments. {060-J04}
An au­to­cratic firm, Amit Varma noted, costs so­ci­ety lit­tle: there will be fifty other firms, and it learns or dies. {#fifty}
~ Subsidiarity, Shah said, fol­lows from the same idea: each city knows best what it should do for it­self.

quote.text: There’s a sin­gle big in­sight in two thou­sand years of pol­i­tics and po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy, it is this one sen­tence, dis­per­sion of power.

sections.label: Seventh difference
sections.head: The hundred-year game
sections.caption: time horizons
body: In India, Ajay Shah said, an un­der­de­vel­oped fi­nan­cial sys­tem makes the cost of cap­i­tal very high. Put a high rate into a net present value cal­cu­la­tion and the fu­ture is re­ally not there, so firms are in­evitably short-sighted.
Many in the pri­vate sec­tor, he said, don’t care about five years out, be­cause they will have sold the com­pany to the next buyer within three years. {#threeyears}
Government must play a longer game. India is on a hun­dred-year jour­ney to close a 9x gap with America in per capita GDP. {#gap}
## Down the pipe­line

Reform, Shah said, runs through a pipe­line: data and re­search, the­o­ries of change, a lively pub­lic de­bate, ex­pert com­mit­tees, the draft­ing of laws, and then state ca­pac­ity, with process man­u­als and train­ing. {060-C15}
It takes 10 to 20 years to make a ma­te­rial dif­fer­ence in any field, a rhythm most of the pri­vate sec­tor is not used to. {#pipeline}

Amit Varma brought the frame home. Think about life over the long­est hori­zon, he said, and live it over the short­est, be­cause life is a suc­ces­sion of days. He quoted Annie Dillard: “How you spend your days is, of course, how you spend your life.” {060-J19}
~ He used to make the mis­take, he said, of fix­ing on awards to win and books to write.

quote.text: There is a pol­icy pipe­line and it is in­ex­orable. It is a damn pipe­line.
It’s not enough to be a democ­racy. You need to be a re­pub­lic where you have a con­sti­tu­tion pro­tect­ing the peo­ple from the state, not the other way around.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Judgment withheld, a puzzle solved, two rules and a test

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a writer he loves and a story he can’t judge
stories.head: The other stories we don’t know
body: Amit Varma has spo­ken on the show be­fore about Alice Munro’s short sto­ries and what she means to him. Then the news broke. {060-R05}

Munro’s daugh­ter had said that her mother’s sec­ond hus­band abused her when she was nine, and that Munro turned a blind eye and did noth­ing. For peo­ple who love her work, Varma said, it brought com­pli­cated emo­tions. Some peo­ple rushed to judg­ment.
Before his flight to DC, where he was record­ing episodes, his friend Shruti Rajagopalan mes­saged him. She is a Munro fan too, and she was dis­turbed. So was he.
On the plane he read David Brooks’s *How to Know a Person*, a book that echoed what Varma had learned from long-form pod­cast­ing about lis­ten­ing and long con­ver­sa­tions. {060-R03}

Brooks writes about Vivian Gornick’s *Fierce Attachments*, in which Gornick and her mother live al­most at cross pur­poses, un­der­stand­ing each other com­pletely, and yet not at all. He uses it to show the com­plex­ity of human be­ings, and why we should not al­ways jump to judg­ment.

On the flight, Varma de­cided. He would keep lov­ing Munro’s work and with­hold judg­ment on her. “Because the world is too com­plex,” he said. “We know one story. We don’t know the other story. We don’t know the other sto­ries.” {060-S05}

~ He was clear that Munro, in min­imis­ing her daughter’s grief, did some­thing “clearly wrong at many lev­els”. And while he sep­a­rates art from artist, there are writ­ers, like Pablo Neruda, he will never read “be­cause I know too much about them”. {060-J20}
stories.why: Most of the time we know only one ver­sion of a messy human story. Withholding judg­ment, with­out ex­cus­ing what was wrong, can be wiser than a rush to con­demn or de­fend.
stories.postscript: It does not mat­ter much ei­ther way, Varma added: Munro is gone, and “it’s not like I’m hav­ing din­ner with her”.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma sets a puzzle, and Ajay Shah does the sums
stories.head: Fifteen minutes, by arithmetic
body: Talk of celebrity cul­ture re­minded Amit Varma of a ques­tion he had set at a quiz about 15 years ago. A good quiz ques­tion, he said, is one where you can work out the an­swer. {060-S03}
He read it out to Ajay Shah. “X is a unit of hype. One kilo X is equal to 10.42 days. One mega X is equal to 28.5 years. What is X?” {060-J11}

Shah worked aloud: 0.01 days, about 864 sec­onds. Twelve min­utes, four­teen? Round it up, Varma said: fif­teen min­utes of fame. X is the Warhol, after Andy Warhol’s line that ev­ery­one in the world will be fa­mous for fif­teen min­utes.
~ Shah struck back: what is a mil­li­he­len? Helen’s was the beauty that launched a thou­sand ships, so a mil­li­he­len is the beauty that will launch one ship. “Nice one,” said Varma. {060-J08}
stories.why: Varma’s idea of quizzing: a ques­tion you ei­ther know or don’t is “damn bor­ing” for peo­ple who aren’t into trivia. A good one re­wards rea­son­ing over re­call, so that any­one with a men­tal cal­cu­la­tor can play.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Warhol, a unit of hype

stories.kicker: Amit Varma applies rules versus deals to his own life
stories.head: House rules for one
body: Rules ver­sus deals, Amit Varma said, is a use­ful frame be­yond coun­tries and firms. Handling peo­ple per­son by per­son takes a lot of cog­ni­tive en­ergy and leads to mis­takes, so he sets him­self rules. {060-S02}
The first: avoid neg­a­tiv­ity. A new ac­quain­tance who com­plains about oth­ers and takes a vic­tim­hood at­ti­tude in­stead of a can-do one is best avoided, in real life and on Twitter.

The sec­ond con­cerns only his own be­hav­iour: lis­ten, try to fig­ure out the other person’s story, and do not make him­self the cen­tre of it. He does not al­ways suc­ceed. “One is male and hard­wired like a male, we are the cen­tre of the uni­verse, but one can make an ef­fort.” {060-J10}
~ The rules one lives by, he said, might be a sub­ject for an­other episode.
stories.why: Deciding in ad­vance how to han­dle a whole class of sit­u­a­tions saves men­tal en­ergy and pre­vents mis­takes, just as, Ajay Shah ar­gued, a state should run on rules rather than case-by-case bar­gains. {060-C12}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his rules for living

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s rule against half-baked opinions
stories.head: Argue it at length or hush
body: The halo ef­fect, Amit Varma said, makes peo­ple as­sume that some­one who ex­cels in one field ex­cels in oth­ers, as if a mi­cro­bi­ol­o­gist could give gyan on any area of medicine. {060-C18}
So these days he gives gyan only on what he has stud­ied well enough. Earlier that same day, in a group con­ver­sa­tion, some­one kept com­ing up with half-baked opin­ions.
Varma spon­ta­neously laid down a rule: “If you state an opin­ion here, you should be able to do an essay length ar­gu­ment for it, oth­er­wise don’t state it.” {060-S04}
~ It sounds a lit­tle ex­treme, he ad­mit­ted. But there is too much cheap opin­ion float­ing around on Twitter, he said, a lot of it re­ceived wis­dom or tribal al­le­giance.
stories.why: A fil­ter against the halo ef­fect and the hot take: speak only on what you have stud­ied well enough to argue at length. People like the hosts, Varma said, should be es­pe­cially care­ful with their opin­ions.

quiz.q: Which three Fs make up Amit Varma’s light triad, set against the dark triad of serial killers?
quiz.a: Firms, fi­nance and free­dom, with fal­lacy nom­i­nated for the dark triad in­stead.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, did stock prices rise during the COVID catastrophe?
quiz.a: Central banks cut rates sharply, so fu­ture cash flows were dis­counted at lower rates.

quiz.q: What is a Warhol, in Amit Varma’s old quiz question?
quiz.a: A unit of hype: fif­teen min­utes of fame, so a kilo-Warhol is 10.42 days.

quiz.q: Whose definition of the state as a monopoly of physical violence did Ajay Shah cite?
quiz.a: Max Weber’s, to show that co­er­cion is core to what a state is.

quiz.q: Why must McDonald’s offer franchisees a standard contract, though no Article 14 binds it?
quiz.a: Deal-by-deal fran­chis­ing would make the or­gan­i­sa­tion fall apart in com­plex­ity and cor­rup­tion.

quiz.q: In Varma’s restaurant analogy, what happens to the diner outvoted by three seafood lovers?
quiz.a: They eat seafood or go hun­gry, even if al­ler­gic to prawns.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 60. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Andy Warhol (Bernard Gotfryd, public domain); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India); Max Weber (Ernst Gottmann, public domain); John Dalberg-Acton, 1st Baron Acton (Allen & Co., public domain); Alice Munro (MacDowell, CC BY-SA 3.0); Paul Graham (Sarah Harlin, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: When McKinsey Comes to Town
shelf.creator: Walt Bogdanich & Michael Forsythe
shelf.why: A cau­tious rec­om­men­da­tion: he finds the book ‘a bit mean’ and ‘one-sided’.

shelf.title: How To Know a Person
shelf.creator: David Brooks
shelf.why: It echoes what Amit learned from long-form pod­cast­ing: the power of long con­ver­sa­tions, of learn­ing to lis­ten, of gen­uine in­ter­est in oth­ers, of in­ten­tion­ally build­ing friend­ships.

shelf.title: Fierce Attachments
shelf.creator: Vivian Gornick
shelf.why: Gornick’s con­stant tus­sle with her mother shows two peo­ple who un­der­stand each other com­pletely and yet not at all.

shelf.title: Alice Munro’s short stories
shelf.creator: Alice Munro
shelf.why: He sep­a­rates art from artist and says he will con­tinue lov­ing her work while with­hold­ing judg­ment on her as a per­son.

shelf.title: The essays of Paul Graham
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Free es­says that Amit calls ‘a trea­sure given to mankind’: mod­els of sim­ple, clear writ­ing, each work­shopped for months, by some­one who also builds things.

shelf.title: The Double ‘Thank You’ Moment
shelf.creator: John Stossel
shelf.why: Stossel’s sim­plest pic­ture of pos­i­tive-sum ex­change: when you buy a cof­fee, you thank the barista and the barista thanks you, be­cause both are bet­ter off.

shelf.title: Is Your Impact Evaluation Asking Questions That Matter? A Four Part Smell Test
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great paper on how to fig­ure out whether a pol­icy has ac­tu­ally made a dif­fer­ence in the world.

shelf.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379)
shelf.creator: The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.why: A deep con­ver­sa­tion with Lant Pritchett on why growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion, drives human wel­fare, why causal­ity runs from de­vel­op­ment to ed­u­ca­tion, and why many RCTs solve small mea­sur­able prob­lems in­stead of mov­ing the nee­dle on poverty.

shelf.title: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (Episode 253, with M.R. Madhavan)
shelf.creator: The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with MR Madhavan on how India’s par­lia­men­tary rules, es­pe­cially the anti-defection law, weaken its democ­racy.

shelf.title: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130, with Rajeswari Sengupta)
shelf.creator: The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.why: Rajeswari Sengupta on what GDP can and can­not mea­sure and how the num­ber is built, in­clud­ing how gov­ern­ment make-work and roads to nowhere in­flate it.

shelf.title: The problems in India’s official data (Episode 21 of Big Ideas)
shelf.creator: Big Ideas, featuring Rajeshwari Sengupta
shelf.why: He cred­its Sengupta with being ‘clever and insightful’ in un­der­stand­ing the dif­fi­cul­ties in India’s GDP mea­sure­ment and telling those sto­ries well.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Episode 45)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: How in­stincts evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes mis­lead us in large, com­plex so­ci­eties: zero-sum think­ing, top-down think­ing, blind­ness to spon­ta­neous order and the pull of strong lead­ers.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: A cri­tique of ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic infrastructure’ such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed mo­nop­o­lies cre­ated by co­er­cive power, with­out checks and bal­ances, that crowd out com­pet­ing pri­vate sys­tems.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Episode 59)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: Why re­search fund­ing in India is ‘a truly bad space’, and the al­ter­na­tive: an in­dus­try-neutral ap­proach that con­tracts R&D out through grants to uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms rather than hav­ing bu­reau­crats pick sec­tors.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: How Indian firms moved from re­gional satraps in the 1980s to top-down ‘imperial’ firms with uni­form best prac­tices, and then to ‘adaptive’ firms that pair rules with local flex­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: India Needs Decentralization (Episode 47)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: The case for sub­sidiar­ity in a coun­try as large and var­ied as India: do as lit­tle as pos­si­ble at the Union level and push power down to cities, where peo­ple can see and talk to the of­fi­cials re­spon­si­ble for their side­walks.

shelf.title: Quizzing is Not Just a Trivial Pursuit
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It sets out his view that good quiz ques­tions are ones you can work out, not ones you ei­ther know or don’t.

shelf.title: Why are firms short-sighted?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It backs Ajay’s ar­gu­ment that a high cost of cap­i­tal in India’s un­der­de­vel­oped fi­nan­cial sys­tem forces firms into short time hori­zons.

shelf.title: The strategy and the tactics
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s own writ­ing on a theme of the episode: gov­ern­ment needs over­all strate­gic think­ing rather than a rush to act.

shelf.title: The Art of Podcasting (Episode 49)
shelf.creator: Everything is Everything
shelf.why: Amit’s fullest think­ing on the craft of pod­cast­ing, which Ajay says also ex­plains how the mod­ern media and cre­ative economies work.

laughs.text: Ajay on a gov­ern­ment-created mo­nop­oly that blocks pri­vate and for­eign com­peti­tors: ‘this is the new Air India. It will sit here, it will lord over the so­ci­ety and peo­ple will clap say­ing, Oh, it is so great India now has planes.’ Amit notes that it sounds dystopian, ex­cept it’s real.

Ajay, de­flat­ing the ‘China model’ buzz: ‘There is noth­ing a Fortune 500 com­pany CEO wants to do more than to fly into a third world coun­try, shake hands with a strong man, and make a deal.’ People call this de­ci­sive gov­ern­ment; he says it should em­bar­rass us.

Ajay’s counter-puzzle to Amit’s Warhol quiz: ‘What is a mil­li­he­len?’ Helen’s was ‘the beauty that launched a thou­sand ships. So mil­li­he­len is the beauty that will launch one ship.’ Amit: ‘Nice one.’

Max Weber’s def­i­ni­tion of the state as a com­mu­nity that achieves and main­tains a mo­nop­oly of phys­i­cal vi­o­lence in a given ter­ri­tory, cited by Ajay to show co­er­cion is the essence of the state.
Lord Acton’s ‘power cor­rupts, ab­so­lute power cor­rupts absolutely’, which Amit uses to ex­plain why the same per­son be­haves dif­fer­ently at the head of a firm and of a gov­ern­ment.
